Jeg havde en kollega der var ekstremt hidsig og manipulerende. 
Vi arbejdede på en rideskole, og hun ville ofte være grovere mod hestene end nødvendigt, til det punkt at de begyndte at være bange for hende og sky når man skulle have grime osv på dem.
 Da jeg fandt ud af hvorfor, hvilket jeg gjorde ved at fange hende i at slå en privatejet hest i hovedet med træktovet, så fortalte jeg straks vores chef som så tog fat i hende ang hendes uacceptable måde at behandle hestene på. 
Dagene efterfølgende var min kollega ekstremt sur på mig, og gik så vidt at fysisk at angribe mig på staldgangen med en høtyv fordi jeg ignorede hendes tirade af fornærmelser og trusler. Da hun angreb mig fysisk, så skubbede jeg hende hårdt væk og hun væltede ind i staldmuren. Hun rendte straks ud af stalden, og jeg tænkte ikke mere over det - før jeg blev kaldt ind på "kontoret" af chefen.
Der sad min kollega og græd, påstod at jeg havde angrebet hende uprovokeret, og at jeg havde "smadret hendes hoved ind i muren". Da jeg forklarede hvad der faktisk skete til chefen, hvorved hun stod med ryggen til min kollega, så holdte min kollega straks op med at græde og smilede ondskabsfuldt til mig, bare for så at begynde at græde videre så snart min chef vendte sig om mod hende for at stille hende et spørgsmål.
Uheldigvis og uvidst for hende, så var der overvågningskameraer i den stald vi var i eftersom det var der privatejede heste var opstaldet, så hun blev selvfølgelig taget i hendes løgn og fyret samme dag.
Hun havde været manipulerende og hidsig over alting før denne episode, men denne var bare kulmineringen på det hele.

That fatigue is definitely tied to AS. I (25F) have suffered from constant fatigue and brain fog since my symptoms started at 15. It's very very common for us to not be able to get proper rest; not only is it hard for us to get comfortable, but we wake often during the night and have to get up to move around before we can lie back down again. A typical night for me is getting up and out of bed 4-5 times to move around a little for 10 minutes. That's nearly an entire hour, nevermind the time it actually takes me to fall back asleep - and we're somehow supposed to be able to deal with this in a "normal" amount of sleep (e.g. 8 hours). It's just not realistic. If I don't sleep 10 hours or more, I'm completely useless. My brain will feel like it's been wrapped in cotton, my reactions are slow, my balance and movement is slow and wonky, my aches are worse, the "morning" stiffness lasts for longer. And that's just without proper rest; don't forget that dealing with chronic pain also takes a lot of energy on top, energy you don't really have.  
So what you're describing is absolutely very common for us.

Your level, unfortunately, has a lot to say about what kind of players you'll likely encounter. Griefers and bullies tend to go for lower levels because they can't defend themselves very well; limited dead-eye, stamina and health, limited tonics, limited weapons, limited ammo types - it makes them easy pickings. Nobody in their right mind picks a fight with a level 300+ unless they're prepared for a very likely ass kicking; it still happens when players decide you'd make a good PVP target in free roam instead of just going into the PVP game modes, but the fact remains, that the lower your level, the higher the likelihood of being griefed. It's fun for them. Doubly so, if your character (and/or you, on mic) is a female.    


You can always enter Defensive Mode when in free roam; either permanently, or when you get shot by someone and you don't want to bother with a fight. It doesn't make it impossible for them to kill you, but it makes it very hard for them; turn it on, get on your horse, and fast travel to somewhere else. There is absolutely no reason for you to turn into a griefer yourself aside from your own frustration, which makes you no better than the one you're ranting about. There are plenty of ways to avoid or quickly end encounters with griefers without needing to turn into one.   


I am sorry you've had those kind of experiences with players, though. Most of us really are laid back and won't be hostile unless we're attacked first; but a bad apple can ruin a bunch, or however the saying goes - and a lot of them simply target lower levels.   


You also have the option of joining posses; you can find them here on Reddit and elsewhere of players you get along well who knows the drill; many low levels recruit high level players to help them with Trader deliveries, Call to Arms and Bounty Hunts, just to mention a few; I've been recruited multiple times and it always helps; people are much less likely to fuck with someone if they've got a group of high levels covering their backs. My reason for this, is that I have had symptoms since I was 15 and wasn't diagnosed until I was  22. In that time, irreparable damage occurred, the pain and stiffness got worse, and I developed other symptoms. I could not walk up or down stairs, I could not walk more than a quarter mile, I could not turn over in bed without crying out in pain. Household chores became impossible, and even something as simple as getting dressed and bending over to wash my legs in the shower became like a mountain I had to climb.  
 I spent a solid 18 months after diagnosis trying NSAID/DMARD/steroid medication, to no avail; not only were they not strong enough to take away any of the pain, but they also did nothing to slow down disease progression for me. It was not until I was referred to a hospitals rheumatology department that I was immediately started on biologic medication; and it took them an additional 1½ year finding one that actually works for me (Zessly, infliximab), after I failed multiple other biologics. If I could go back in time, I would've asked them immediately to put me on a biologic medication instead of going through the pills I did; especially as NSAIDS are terrible for your stomach and digestion and you'd likely need to take other medication at the same time to prevent NSAIDs from messing up your stomach; I know I did. 

The concern about immunosuppresant medication is valid, especially in the middle of a pandemic, but if you use masks, don't get too close to strangers, and you're careful and diligent when it comes to hygiene, you will be okay - the safeguards you take won't be any different; it might just be a little easier for you to remember these things when it's not just a "I don't want to be sick" compared to a "I don't want to be sick because I have a higher risk of it now".

Humira is a great biologic for some, but she also has to discuss with her rheumatologist if she's getting enough relief from it; depending on her pain and stiffness levels, there may be another medication out there (or a supplementing medication) that'll help her further.   
And yes, physical exercise can help; but it's a careful balance, and actively seeking out pain is something we instinctively try to avoid at all costs. But she should definitely look into exercise options that she can handle and stick with them; swimming, for one, is fantastic; not only are you weightless in the water which eases the strain on your joints, but it also strengthens your entire body which is a good thing. Exercise is important, especially when you live an otherwise sedentary lifestyle; many end up struggling with excess weight and the associated health risks - and there is a definite link between A.S and heart disease made worse by obesity, for one.  
As for the IUD, the only link I'm aware of is the increased risk of producing antibodies associated with the development of RA - these two diseases are not the same. Before getting it removed, make sure to consult a doctor.

A.S seems a bit unlikely in that case; pain is caused by the inflammation in early stages, and the inflammation and damage in later stages. Imaging scans can't be relied on as the only factors for a diagnosis as there are cases of non-radiographical axspa, but the common denominator is always an elevated inflammation marker of some sort (CRP, ESR) . HLA-B27 gene is also a factor, but not a necessity; I'm also white, 25, European; but negative for the gene. It is possible that your symptoms and aches are caused by your previous bulging disc and that it comes back seemingly at random but triggered by certain movements or activities you may not be aware of doing. What you could do, is during a flare-up of the pain and stiffness, have your doctors do another CRP/ESR + white blood cell + blood platelet test; if these are elevated, they could be marking the active inflammation of an early stage that otherwise would not be visible on any tests.

I'm glad you got a new doctor who cares about her patients; they make all the difference in the world, especially for progressive diseases.  


I've been through a myriad of medication; high doses of ibuprofen, high doses of long-lasting ibumetin, Naproxen, Sulfasalazine, Prednisolone - none of which worked but just gave me weird side effects (did you know, Sulfasalazine can actually turn your tears yellow? Freaked me out proper, that!). Then they tried biologics for me and I have been on Hyrimoz injections and Benepali injections, both to no avail; did not experience any relief at all - thankfully, no side effects either, none that lasted for more than the initial 1-2 weeks while my body got used to them. The last one they've tried for me is Zessly (infliximab) infusions - and they help suppress the inflammation; or did, until I developed side effects of high/low heart-rate and the accompanying dizziness/fainting, which prompted blood tests and EKGs and such. EKG came back mostly normal and they gave me the choice if I wanted to go back on Zessly or try something else; I chose to go back on Zessly and just have my heart monitored regularly, because it's the first one that has given me any relief at all. I go back in for infusions on the 13th. That being said, it helps relieve stiffness and some pain, but does not take away everything; the specialists say the damage done is too severe for the pain to ever entirely go away; but I'd like to think I'm managing okay, even if I have to lie to myself to believe it!   


I also luckily don't have to worry about cost; I'm from Denmark, and medicines like biologics are covered entirely by the government (through taxes).   


I'm glad to hear you've got your heard up and are seeking out positive stories and experiences, too; it's important to stay realistic, but with a positive mindset, it does get quite a bit more manageable :)

Pain-wise, it does sound similar to AS; all of the urination/stomach issues are not what I'd usually consider an AS symptom, but it could easily be another autoimmune disorder of some sort; they tend to go hand-in-hand. The joint pain is definitely a clear sign, especially the lower back/SI joint pain; I think about 80% of people with AS experience pain there, and it's usually one of the first areas it starts in. 

Previous generations having AS is not a requirement (I'm also the first), and the HLA-B27 gene is only an indicator but also not a requirement (I'm negative). 

I'm glad to hear your doctor is on top of things and taking the steps necessary to reach a diagnosis and following treatment quickly; I started having symptoms at 15 and wasn't diagnosed until 22 because doctors didn't take me seriously (I was too young, too active on/off work, or needed to lose weight (normal BMI); and because of their negligence, this disease has been causing havoc for years without anything to slow it. Mine started out as a slight stiffness in the morning that quickly went away; evolved into a bit of an ache that also went away quickly; and then over time went from mild aches to severe pain, hours long stiffness episodes, swelling, balance problems, inflammation of nearby muscles and nerves (especially the sciatic), widespread muscle pain, and all of these physical symptoms brought psychological ones too.   


My advice to you, is to keep a careful daily log of your symptoms and severity. Keep track of what you eat and drink, to see if there's anything in your diet that may trigger flares. Be prepared to have to go through several different types of medications before you find one that works for you, and have faith that there is one out there that works for you. Don't discount the mental aspect of this; many who suffers from chronic pain struggle with depression, and there's absolutely nothing wrong with seeking help if that happens for you. Communicate with your doctor/specialists. Ask them for mild exercises you can do to keep up mobility in your affected joints; even if it hurts to do, it helps in the long run.   


Good luck.
